comments.text:
Honestly, I got this card in a haste for eqv. Of USD250 (card prices in here are always more than international. I had a 4460 i5, GTX960, and went to the shop to see if it was still working, as I had issues booting up before it was left unused. Planning to only change the case, but when we tried to turn it on, nothing turns on, so we thought mobo and CPU got busted due to bad electrical grounding in my house. After changing mobo and CPU, with my old GPU, my GTX960 turned out to be busted too. The shop recommended 1650 DDR6, but I knew it was an older card. Then I searched quickly for a GPU around the same price, and got the RX6500XT, and at quick glance, average FPS for all games were higher, and didn't bother to read anything else. Wasn't even planning to buy a new CPU anyway. For the price and FPS, I pulled the trigger. 

3 days in, I'm actually happy with it. I don't play as much heavy games, and only at 1080p. NFS is what I'm playing currently, and it constantly gets 60FPS or above. I did notice that for example, trees were suddenyl popping up. Maybe because of the low bandwidth? And it does kind of slow to load, with some items suddenly popping up. I'm not really sure of the technicalities. 

All said, I'm still happy, and I think it's still a big upgrade coming from GTX960 (2GB VRAM mind you). Didn't really know other alternatives, and I don't want to risk on buying second hand cards. GTX1650 was recommended to me, but I saw it was a much older card so I didn't want it.

 I don't really do rendering and streaming. I have an M1 macbook for photo and video editing, so my PC is solely for gaming (for now atleast). So for what it is and the price in my country, its still worth it if you focus solely on gaming, and nothing else.

Second, Theres no way to compare the rx 6500xt with the gtx 1650, theres no worse card than the 1650, AND NOBODY SAID OR SAYS NOTHING ABOUT IT. The 1650 performs worse than a 1060 3gb, rx 570 and even an rx 480 FOR THE SAME PRICE OF THE RX 6500XT. In conclusion, for its price and performance the rx 6500xt is a great option for gaming at 1080 (60% of the steam users use this resolution) at high-med settings. And its the best option in the market for its price range (11/04/2021).

comments.text:
There's lots of talk here about how the performance will be garbage when this card is bought to upgrade an older rig. And that's true, but it's not AMD's target market. the RX 6500XT is following in the footsteps of the RX 5500, RX 550, RX 450 etc. as being the step-up "real video card" in corporate and low-end home systems that would otherwise make due with integrated video. The Dell Optiplex, HP Pro and Elite, Lenovo ThinkCentre, and so on. As such, AMD is intending it to end up largely in new systems, paired with CPUs and motherboards supporting PCIe gen 4. 

Anthony alluded to the tested XFX card having an over-designed cooler; Don't be surprised to see this GPU end up on cards in low-profile form-factors, and/or with substantially more "appropriate" cooling solutions. I also wouldn't be surprised if they roll cards without the PCIe power connector, either by under-clocking the GPU, or straight-up violating the PCIe power delivery spec.

Just see number of gpu.
Nvidia: 1070 - First 2 digits show generation (8,9,10,20,30 latest), 10th generation and 70 means high end GPU.

Last 2 digits: 10-30 office PCs
50-60 mid end/budget gaming cards
70-80 high end
90 Top tier
Ti/Super : Cards which are slightly faster than their non ti/ non super models.

In AMD, It's similar:
rx 580, rx 6900 xt

first digit: Generation (400,500,5000, 6000 latest)
Last 2 digits: 10-40 Office PCs
50-60 budget gaming
60-70 mid end
70-90 high end

XT: Faster than non-XT models.

comments.text:
@thatslegit  They thought it was a shameless cash grab because different Youtubers, who follow technology and do reviews, fail to understand that out in the world there's at LEAST 15% inflation on pretty much everything, and on some things, 25%, 50% and I see things I used to buy closer to 2X the cost they used to be.  Is this EVERY company doing a cash grab?

No it's called inflation driven by many factors.  Prices have been increasing since the beginning of 2020, but increased a lot in 2021, and while some tech youtubers said companies aren't making low end products because they're too busy making money on high end products, the reality is the 6500 XT.  This is REALLY the best AMD can do for $200.  Their production costs have increased substantially.  Shipping costs are more.  For GPUs in particular, they almost all come out of China and both the EU countries and the US put large import taxes on them, in the EU it's a VAT that ranges between 20 - 25% depending on the country, and the US it's a 25% tariff.  These companies pay that tariff.  It started Jan 1, 2021.  Companies said their prices were going to go up because of it.  Did people not believe them?  So, today's price of $200 USD is like $140 back in 2017.  That's how much inflation along with a 25% import tax is affecting companies now.  So, for price, the 6500 XT compares to the RX-460 and the 1050 Ti, both around $140 when released.  The math is simple.  140 + 15% inflation gets you to $160.  160 + 25% import taxes gets you to $200.  This product beats the snot out of an RX-460 and 1050 Ti, so based on how bad inflation has been, there's improvement at the same price point once inflation and new taxes are added in.

It's up to individuals to follow what's going on in the world and not listen to Youtubers who review products for their living who talk about things they DON'T study, such as the global economy, taxes, etc....

In the US inflation has been driven by Covid.  Millions of people dropped out of the workforce, mostly because of homeschooling or children being at home for online schooling.  Homeschooling in the US grew from 5% to 10% during Covid.  And, if I even have to comment about how many disruptions to schools Covid has created, then people have their heads in the sand.  Schools are constantly disrupted by high rates of infection and then they close the school for a time period and students have to learn via online classes.  So, this is millions of parents that USED to be in the workforce and now gone.  All across the country businesses are trying to get people.  There's a shortage of about 40,000 truck drivers.  Because of the shortage of workers companies have been raising their wages.  If people don't think that adds cost to products they're stupid.  Of COURSE it does.  But at the same time, Trump passed a huge package of tariffs aimed at China which is where a lot of goods sold in the US are manufactured.  Many got exemptions, until after 2020, probably because HE didn't want inflation to hit hard right before the election.  The exemptions ended Jan 1, 2021.  Biden chose to leave them in place with very few exceptions.  The EXEC got sued by one business group over the tariff on solar panels and the EXEC lost in a trade court.  They didn't appeal, because they'd look stupid and like hypocrites trying to make solar panels cost 25% more when you're pushing a green energy agenda.

So most things that come out of China into N. America get a 25% tariff slapped on it, and anyone who can do simple math should understand that's 25% inflation right there, before other costs affect the product.

But, moving products around in the US and really N. America costs a bit more because of truck drivers making a bit more money and the shortage of drivers.  Retailers are paying out more payroll as most have raised their pay rates.  Amazon for instance increased wages for warehouse workers by 25% due to Covid.  Before Covid they used to start at around $12 USD/hr.  Now they start at $16 USD/hr.  So, regardless of a retailer being online or brick and morter or both, wages have risen and it inflates prices.

In other words, EVERY part of producing a product, shipping it from Asia to N. America, getting it from a point of entry to a retailer, the retailer dealing with the product, and then shipping it to you, has gone up.  Every entity has to get more money to make a similar profit.

For some reason many Youtubers can't figure this one out, and maybe it's because many products just show up at their door for free and for lower cost items they don't have to repack it and send it to someone else.  So while they SAY they feel the consumer's pain, they've done zero work to understand costs, and take the easy path of blaming AMD, Nvidia and all their partner companies.  Even LTT has short term memory.  They covered the tariff and how it's affecting prices back in Feb 2021, but for some reason Anthony does a video, talks about inflation affecting cost, but then fails to remember he's talking about a GPU, where most come out of China and subject to 25% import taxes now, where before Trump the US believed in free trade for the most part.

And yes I have a list of links that covers everything I said for those who haven't followed the news.

So, AMD, Nvidia, MSI, ASUS, etc.... are both the exporter and importer on GPUs coming from China to the US, and even if they use a 3rd party, they pay the tariff.

And I could go on.  I think most people realize that due to port of entry backups, shipping companies are charging more money.


So yeah, Youtubers who want to keep bashing AMD and Nvidia are part of the problem because they give a false impression of what's happening in the world.  AMD didn't make the cost of bacon or coffee beans that I buy go up by almost 100%.  Covid and the reaction to it did.

Example the textures and models are loading in on the one buffer. (single 64 lane) The textures load first in the clock cycle and then the models but they are only 32 bit each . comments.text:
You mentioned inflation, but failed to mention that the importers of the GPUs, which are the companies themselves, so MSI, Gigabyte, XFX, ASUS, etc... are also paying a stiff tariff on products coming out of China, and GPUs come out of China.  Youtubers need to stop forgetting about this because you're giving an impression that all these companies are scalping the consumer, and they're not.  So, if this would have a $175 USD GPU when imported, add 25%.  It's now about a $220 USD GPU.  Considering inflation is so high, these companies are paying about 10 - 15% more to make the GPUs, so these GPU are being made for a price level that would have been similar to a $150 USD GPU 2 years ago, and more like a $135 GPU going back 4 years ago.

And this is what Youtubers keep forgetting.  And it's not just the US that charges such a large import tax, the EU countries do too, with a Value added tax the importers also pay and ranges from 20 - 25%.  So, these large taxes, that didn't exist a few years ago are what's making the largest price increase.  Inflation is global and yes it makes something that would have been something cost $175 USD 4 years ago, cost $200 USD now, because inflation since 2017 is EASILY 15%, and probably more.


So, stop blaming AMD and Nvidia.  This is what you get now for $200 USD, and that MSRP will be short lived because these companies can't make enough profit at that price, so that's a FAKE MSRP.  It probably needs to cost closer to $250 USD.  So sad, too bad.  

Compared to 4 years ago, a $200 USD GPU NOW, would have cost about $140 4 years ago.  That's how hard inflation (15%) along with tariffs (25%) is making it on these companies to sell an inexpensive GPU.  So even comparing this GPU to an RX-580 is a bit of a stretch.  Maybe an RX-550 is closer for price point.

comments.text:
@LinusTechTips  Man I made a long reply to this and now it's gone.  No, companies are now baking in that tariff into the MSRP if they have to pay it, and once again the EU countries are also adding a 20 - 25% VAT on imports from certain countries, and it's added to GPUs.  And I don't know if they have the distinction on coming from either Taiwan or China, and if the GPU doesn't get assembled in China, it most likely gets assembled in Taiwan.

The importer pays the tariff, and companies like MSI, AMD, Nvidia, ASUS, XFX, Gigabyte, etc.... are all international companies.  They are both the importer and exporter.  Ampere and RDNA 2 launched at the end of 2020, before the tariff went into place.  Those MSRPs got shot out the window once tariffs hit, and now global inflation on EVERYTHING is affecting the cost of the raw materials, the manufacturing of parts, the essembly, shipping to different countries, and the logistics of moving the parts around in any country, along with higher costs for the retailers so THEY need to make more money too.

I can't speak to Canada, but in the US we are short tens of thousands of truck drivers, and the ones being hired in are making a bit more money.  Every company, even online companies are paying employees more money, and in some cases it's about 25% more than when Covid hit.  Amazon warehouse workers are making $16/hr starting.  Before Covid that was more like $12 USD/hr.  Retailers are paying more payroll.

So EVERYTHING costs more money.  You can't look at that price on newegg and say where that price came from because there are too many things making the price higher.


But, the things I said are backed up with data.  For the tariff the importer pays:

https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-trade-tariffs-explainer-idUSKCN1SB0UF#:~:text=The%20CBP%20typically%20requires%20importers%20to%20pay%20the,of%20foreign%20companies%20that%20import%20goods%20from%20China.

"A tariff is a tax on imports. The CBP typically requires importers to pay the duties within 10 days of their shipments clearing customs."

The fact that all these companies raised their prices:

While some GPUs do come out of Taiwan, I'm pretty sure most come out of China.  The heat sinks, fan assemblies, probably PCBs along with other parts come from China and China is a big market for lower cost GPUs especially.

On top of that, companies that make more premium GPUs are no longer accepting smaller margins for their products just because AMD and Nvidia want them to keep their pricing close to the MSRPs that AMD and Nvidia set, and you can expect these products to be $150 to $200 USD more than a product priced near that MSRP.

comments.text: @Jman116Films  Wrong. I made the mod myself with help from forum posts and it wasn't hard because my card has dual BIOS, so I wasn't worried about bricking it. I tweaked the VRAM timings to get from 169GB/s(stock timings at 1750mhz) to 223GB/s(tweaked timings at 2050mhz) in oclmembench. A regular RX580 scores around 186GB/s stock at 2000mhz. It's worth knowing that Polaris is very memory-starved so tweaking the VRAM leads to massive gains. My XFX model came with Samsung 2000mhz RAM, so it was easy to clock it at 2050mhz. I also overclocked the core by 70mhz while cutting the voltage by 90mv. All in all, I'm getting 10-15% more FPS, depending on game and benchmark and power consumption has gone down to only about 120-130W max. In LuxMark 3.1(OpenCL benchmark, very memory-bound), my 570 is actually beating most 580s and even a few 590s.

You mean because you believe the stupidity?

AMD cut GPU production.  You know that right?  They shifted it to make core chiplets for  EPYC CPUs, which is where AMD is making a KILLING.  THAT is why they have record profits.  Never has AMD been the major provider of X86-64 CPUs until Zen 2 EPYC, and Zen 3 EPYC is substantially better than Zen 2 EPYC.  Along with those sales comes contracts.  This is big money, and it's why Intel has always made great profits.

Both AMD and Intel both don't make large profits off of consumer CPUs and the same is true for AMD and GPUs.  Intel USED to make large profits off of consumer CPUs until enthusiasts started switching to AMD, like, in LARGE numbers, enough to shift the market share to mostly AMD, and it only took 3 years.  So Intel and AMD both make reasonable profits on their consumer CPUs.

Nvidia is the company who's made the most profits on consumer GPUs, not AMD, and right now BOTH companies are struggling more than you think.  Sure they're making more profit now, but global inflation has affected both companies, so to have a similar profit to 2 years ago, in terms of % of profit, they HAVE to be making more profit now than 2 years ago because of how much inflation has grown.  Their profit margins for GPUs are similar to 2 years ago.

Both companies really can barely afford to make a budget GPU.  Inflation is about 15% over just TWO YEARS ago, and for some products, if you haven't noticed, inflation is 50 - 100% over 2 years ago.  So, start with something that would have cost $140 USD 2 years ago to produce.  Add 15% due to everything costing more to make the GPU, EVERY component, down to each tiny transistor.  140 now becomes  $160 USD.  Now, and this is the part people keep wanting to forget about, add 25%, because that's what AMD, Nvidia, MSI, ASUS, XFX, Gigabyte, etc..... are having to pay to import products from China into the US and the EU.  For the US, it's a 25% tariff that went into place Jan 1, 2021 and ALL these companies said will cause their prices to go up, and for the EU, the different countries have a 20 - 25% VAT.  In both cases the importer pays it.  The importer are these companies.  So, now take that $160 GPU that used to cost $140, and add on that tariff.  160 + 25% = $200 USD.  

This video and every other one keep wanting to ignore current economics, and it's clear that people are sticking their heads in the sand about what's happening.  And yet, LTT talked about this VERY point back in Feb 2021 in a video talking about the US tariff.

comments.text:
I’m not impressed with AMD’s or nVidia’s response to this GPU shortage. They appear to be offering new cards that are so under powered that not only do crypto miners have no use for them, gamers don’t either because nobody wants to play games at 15 fps with ray tracing or 45 without. And the issue is further compounded by the fact that as newer games are released with fancier engines and graphical assets, average FPS declines on the same hardware. This 6500 XT is barely hitting 45-50 fps now, but in a year it might be 35-40 and just get lower from there the year after. This isn’t even a side grade, it’s a straight up $200 downgrade.

Rather than use the limited amount of silicon during this shortage to make under powered cards like 6500 XT, why not use that silicon to pump out more cards that people actually want from the current gen lineup, like new 3070/3080 Tis or 6700/6800 XTs? The miners already have their current gen cards and won't be buying anything new unless it starts with 4 or 7 for nVidia or AMD respectively. This is an opportunity for both teams to save some cash on R&D by focusing on pumping out more current gen cards that gamers can actually buy rather than rushing out more next gen paper launches that nobody can buy.

comments.text:
Except, that old world is gone.  GPUs coming off the line right now are 30 - 35% more expensive than even 2 years ago.  It's not just the 15% inflation that Anthony mentioned, it's also large import taxes going into the largest markets outside of China.  The EU countries add a VAT that's 20 - 25%, and the US adds a tariff that's 25%, which also affects the Canadian market.  Companies like AMD, Nvidia, ASUS, XFX, MSI, Gigabyte, etc... are the importers.  These are all international companies.  They are both the exporter and importer, even if some other company is involved in the actual shipping.  They are still the ones who are paying the cost.

This is the best you're going to get for $200 USD and you won't find it at that cost anyway, because every entity along the supply chain including the retailers whether they're online or brick and mortar adds more cost than 2 years ago.  I bought a few 1660 Supers and very glad I did

Depending on where you live, this won't get fixed until GPU manufacturing is significant outside of China, so GPUs for the Chinese market can be made in China, and GPUs for other countries can be made outside of China.  That would get rid of the large import taxes.  With a lot of 5nm and whatever node Intel will be ready with in 2024 - 2025 coming online, it will help to meet GPU demand, as long as the assembly and construction of parts needed for GPUs has been ramped up for production outside of China.  

But this won't solve the inflation problem, which by then could be about 25%.

So, reality is, for low end, graphics cards will be a terrible buy and it doesn't matter if it's AMD or Nvidia.  Intel and AMD's APUs will be a lot better in a couple years and that's going to be gaming at the low end in the future.  Both companies have software to make those APUs run well for gaming, with RSR or FSR for AMD and I forget what Intel's package is called.

And, a 1650 Super is $500 now.  It doesn't matter what you could get something for in the past.  It matters what you can get it for now.

comments.text:
@DimiS1978  I watched his video where he tested the 5500 XT using both gen 3 and gen 4 and he limited the lanes.  Yes I saw the difference. But at the same time, the 4GB memory size and the bandwidth of that memory ALSO affects fps as is clearly shown.  In both cases not all games are affected.

So, what I said is if the game is being affected from stepping down to PCIe gen3 X4, then it is also probably being affected by the 4GB of memory anyway, so, there's that.  Either way you're feeding memory or using data stored in the memory, right?

I'm not going to do a long drawn out discussion of current economics, but this GPU should have been compared to a 1050 Ti and an RX-460, because of how much both inflation and tariffs are affecting the cost.  It's almost impossible right now to think the way we used to think about products because there are too many things affecting prices.  Inflation is making EVERY component that goes into making a GPU more expensive, so you should expect that there's at least a 15% higher cost to make a similar product than in 2017.  Shipping costs more.  There's a 25% tariff on GPUs coming out of China into N. America, and most come out of China.  The EU countries has a 20 - 25% VAT added to various imports and GPUs fall into that. From here I'll stick with the U.S. since I live there and I pay attention to the news.  The country is short tens of thousands of truck drivers.  The ones getting hired along with current drivers are making a bit more money.  Higher cost.  If there are middlemen, like some companies use suppliers, THEY charge more money.  ALL retailers are paying more payroll, and that includes Amazon and newegg.  In the case of Amazon they're paying about 25% more for their workers than before Covid hit.  So, every part of producing a GPU and getting it from where it was assembled to you, costs more.

This part would be similar to something that cost $140 USD back in 2017, not an RX-580 that cost more than $200 USD when it was released.

So, you can't expect much from budget GPUs.  There are too many cuts that have to be made to sell the product at a price point people would consider for a budget GPU.

And Steve from HDWU is the LAST person in the world to understand this point and always wants to blame the companies that make the products like AMD and Nvidia, but there's nothing they can do.  It's why it took them so long to put out a budget part and I'm sure neither company wanted to for this reason EXACTLY.  They have to save money  in any way possible to put out a low end GPU to have it only cost $200 USD MSRP.  Now, I know when you constantly hear that companies don't want to put out budget parts because they can screw over consumers, you're going to start believing it so I expect you to believe the nonsense, but I'm sorry once again I follow news and it should be blatantly obvious to people that EVERYTHING costs more now.  Not things that have been sitting on shelves for a year, but for new products coming out they all cost more to make than 2 years ago and it's not a trivial thing.

So no, I quit watching Steve's videos.  I think he's out of touch when it comes to global economics and says too many things I don't like.  Tim on the other hand, when doing they're end of month Q&As seemed to say things that I could tell he understands what's happening and subtly contradicts Steve so I watch his videos.  But I think he's now getting into the bashing of companies more so really, I'm just not a fan.  I want data points without opinion and commentary.

And finally, and I know people will hate this statement, people who bought a B450 after companies were talking about PCIe gen4, which was talked about before 2019 and was known it would be incorporated into Zen 2, should have realized issues could arise from sticking with a gen 3 MB.  I do understand B450 and X470 have been around since before the discussion of gen4, but if you bought a gen3 board knowing GPU makers are going to start using gen4, that's on you, and also on the people who gave you recommendations.  I didn't buy B450 boards to build systems for gaming.  I bought X570 and bore the cost because I bought those to be gaming systems for many years.  If you buy a budget system, expect it to be a budget system, and I don't know how to say it better than that.  I've built systems using B450 boards, but I didn't build them for people who were going to be gaming on them.  They make an excellent budget system.  However, if they want to spend the money to upgrade their GPU, in which case it would be a 16 lane GPU, they CAN and it will run fine, but I built most of those using Zen+ CPUs so they'd have to upgrade their CPU if they want an excellent gaming rig.  And, I also don't take recommendations from people who talk about switching systems out all the time.  I build a system for myself to last many years so once I get it going I don't have to worry about it, and the only thing I'll switch out is a GPU when I feel the cost is worth the gaming improvement.  Most Youtubers try to justify switching out parts or systems.  And, because AMD can have a platform that can accept multiple gens of CPUs, I tend to buy a 2nd gen MB on that new platform and a lower cost CPU, knowing I'm going to upgrade the CPU with the last gen it will work with.

And for the poor souls that buy into Intel, knowing they're buying a single or two generation product, well once again, that's on you so don't cry about it.

@offpoynt4747  It's not a matter of trying to justify anything, or at least people who realize that there's global inflation, that over the last 2 years is more than 15% and in some countries is more like 50%.  To compare this to an RX-580 is totally out of touch with current economics.  It's comparible to something that would have cost $140 USD back in 2017. That would be an RX-460 or a GTX 1050 Ti.  And, this beats the snot out of both of those GPUs.  So why $140?  Actually I think this is very conservative, but start with that price, add 15% and you get to $160.  Back in 2017 the US didn't have a tariff on GPUs coming out of China.  There was one added in 2018 or 2019, but Trump put a hold on tariffs on many products until Jan 1, 2021.  THAT tariff is simply destroying the ability for a company to produce a low budget GPU and until that tariff is removed it's better to buy an APU, especially when Zen 4 and 13th gen exist, as both products will have better APUs.  For AMD they move to RDNA 2.

But, not only is the US charging a 25% tariff, and this also affects Canada as Linus pointed out in Feb 2021 in a video talking about the US tariff, but the EU ALSO has a VAT on certain imported goods, and GPUs are one of them.  The VAT is country dependent, but varies from 20 - 25%.

https://www.techspot.com/news/92490-nvidia-zotac-urge-us-drop-trump-era-china.html#:~:text=Nvidia%20specifically%20cited%20the%20lack%20of%20GPU%20manufacturing,US%20and%20in%20only%20limited%20amounts%20in%20Taiwan.

https://www.theverge.com/2021/1/7/22217206/nvidia-amd-gpu-trump-tax-china-tariff-exemption-expire


So, I started with a $140 USD product back in 2017, and it's now $160 because of inflation.  Now add in 25%.  You're at $200 USD.  And, this doesn't account for the nightmare logistics problems in the US due to a shortage of about 40,000 truck drivers and the ones who are still there are being paid a lot more and the new hires also.  It doesn't account for retailers having to pay employees more income now, and at Amazon it's about 25% more than what they were paying pre-Covid, and I'm talking about each person, not total payroll.  Before Covid, Amazon was paying a warehouse worker about $12 USD/hr.  They now pay $16 USD/hr.  25% more.  Shippers charge more money, retailers have to make more money so they charge more per product because retailers are paying more for payroll and other costs.  And, you can assume that each one of these entities is charging more than just their added expenses.  Each entity is making more profit because with so much instability it's hard to predict what they need to make down to the last penny.  So, you have a $200 USD MSRP product that gets shipped from China, and it costs more to ship, gets to a point of entry, costs more to get it from there to a retailer, almost always a distribution point, and then get it from a distribution point to a warehouse, or straight to a consumer, for online retailers.  Every step is more expensive.  SO, a $200 USD MSRP product is no longer $200 from the retailer.  It's more like $225 - $240.  But that's not the end all.  Partner companies make GPUs that are more expensive and AMD, Nvidia used to get upset with these companies if their premium products had an MSRP much greater than what AMD, Nvidia listed.  These companies can no longer accept smaller margins.  The premium products can cost a lot more to manufacture, and THOSE products are going to cost $120 - $200 USD more than listed MSRPs.  

So what's real is, people don't want to accept the current reality of the global economy.  It's depressing.  But refusing to accept it ain't going to change the reality of it.

So if you need a budget GPU, you're better off getting an APU for now, and taking advantage of FSR or RSR if you want to play games.  APUs will be better once again for Zen 4 and 13th gen.  So if you're going to build a budget system in the near future, plan on getting an APU because budget GPUs aren't going to be much better, but adds a lot to the cost.  CPUs and APUs don't  have the tariff added since they don't come out of China.  But you better believe that inflation is going to affect Intel 13th gen and Zen 4.

Oh, and did I mention that scalpers and miners create scarcity, and this emboldens every entity in the supply chain to jack their prices since the demand is endless?

Two years ago was an eternity.  The only way those prices are coming back is the EU countries remove their large import taxes, VATs, and the US removes their large import tax, the 25% tariff.  AND, you need a global recession that hurts the economy, makes the demand on everything computers to drop, there is a global job shortage and companies can drop their wages they're paying now, and raw materials drop in price due to all of this.

If you want to call this a justification for anything, I guess, but this is the case for EVERYTHING right now.  I'm paying 2X more for some things that don't even have an issue with supply.  It's all about Covid affecting the jobs and companies having to pay a lot more payroll or more for materials they need, or affecting how they do things to keep the workforce safe.  Bacon is one of those things.  It's almost twice as expensive now in most the US than 1.5 years ago, and there's a lot of goods that are 25 - 50% more expensive.  I'm not buying bacon.  The brand of coffee I've been buying is 2X the cost now.  I'm drinking less coffee and more tea.

comments.text:
@LunarVVolf " Bull effing shit. I look forward to the day AMD fanbois quit making excuses for their deity."

So you don't understand that contracts were made more than a year ago for wafer production with TSMC?  Maybe you need to watch more videos from different channels that talk about wafer production and node technologies.  And, it's node specific, not "I want whatever you got"  There is no such thing as TSMC having extra wafer capacity.  So contracts are specific.  And because of that, the chips that go on these nodes are going to be the ones that were tested for over a year to be on that node.

Yes, this die has been in design for a few years.  The contract with TSMC doesn't specify specific ICs to be made, but it is based on wafer allocation.  It's not any different for any other company that's a fabless chipmaker.  In the case of Nvidia, their contract is with Samsung for wafer production.

That's how the world of chipmaking/fabrication works.

Yes, they could have used a more powerful chip, but then it wouldn't have been a "budget" GPU.

And maybe you forget that with hyperinflation and very stiff import taxes, the cost for ALL GPUs coming out of China, which is most all of them are about 40% more expensive, first with about 15% inflation making them more expensive to make and then a 20 - 25% VAT going into EU countries and a 25% tariff going into the US.  And adding to that,  EVERY part of the supply chain is more expensive.  Shipping from China to the US, higher shipping inside the US due to trucking costs being higher, and retailers needing to make more money off products they sell since they're paying higher wages, so a $200 MSRP GPU leaving China ends up being a $270 USD GPU when you buy it because of how much costs have grown.  Before Covid, Amazon warehouse workers were making about $12/hr.  They're now making $18/hr.  You think Amazon accepts that as a loss?  Not a chance in hell, they charge more money.  That's a 50% increase in the wages they pay out.  Same thing is happening at every retailer, or at least in cities, maybe not small towns.

So this isn't comparable to an RX-580 in terms of cost because of how great inflation and import costs have changed the economics of GPUs out of China.  It's comparable to something that cost $140 USD back in 2017, so an RX460 or a GTX 1050 Ti.  There wasn't a tariff back on 2017 coming into the US.  That was a gift from Trump and kept in place by Biden and went into effect Jan 1, 2021.

But for all the people complaining, these GPUs will sell out and fast and will hit the same demand pressure that every GPU has, except maybe the ones that cost $3000 USD now, like an RTX 3090.  They're probably starting to build up on shelves now.
